description: Slavic Soul Party are Eastern Europe's answer to the funk (and "Grunt") of the J.B.'s or, more recently, the Budos Band. On their recordings, and every Tuesday at Barbès, the 10-person brass ensemble pins Gypsy melodies against the sort of jazzy r&b horn collages you hear in movies adapted from Elmore Leonard books. The best part, though, is how they interact with their audience at their concerts, sometimes breaking the fourth wall, and really making each word in their name—especially the last—pull its weight.

name: Royksopp
description: Playing a round of Canadian and East Coast dates in support of their 2010 release Senior, Norwegian electro duo Royksopp will likely amplify the relatively subdued, squish-tempo tones of that record in a room like Webster. Think of the bright plastic, injection-molded beats of 2009's Junior, say, or maybe those memories of when your European college buddy threw an impromptu glitter and Ajax party in the student union. Wear your Hypercolor.

name: Dub Trio
description: Working simultaneously as crack session players, a go-to support act (for Matisyahu and others), and as their own ferociously expressive act, Brooklyn's Dub Trio has figured out their own way of hybridism in the 21st century. After the acclaim of 2008's Another Sound Is Dying, new material has been surfacing lately in the form of EPs. The format's brevity doesn't make the trio's metal-shop echo and clang any less formidable. With Heldin.

name: Joan La Barbara
description: As though Auto-Tuned at birth, no singer does more unlikely things with her voice--including chordal emissions, ululations, and circular singing--than this venerable, modernist performer/composer. La Barbara will mark St. Patrick's Day with two James Joyce-inspired works by John Cage, "The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs" and "Nowth Upon Nacht." She'll also perform Morton Feldman's tiniest composition, "Only," as well as "Gatekeeper" for "amplified voice and sonic atmosphere" from her opera-in-progress inspired by Virginia Woolf and Joseph Cornell.

name: Crystal Castles
description: We'd be glad to write off Crystal Castles as neon-hoodie-scene succubi, but their second eponymous record was just too sharp, too similar to lucid dreaming. Their newly evolved sonic distortion and blissful melancholia has cemented them as the band too good to hate. Tonight's show at Terminal 5 is sold out, don't you know, so take pleasure in the mysterious chemistry of Ethan Kath and Alice Glass as they scream and discombobulate to their hearts' content. With Teengirl Fantasy.

name: British Sea Power
description: After over a decade in existence, it looks like this sweeping, dynamic indie band is finally coming into its own. 2007's Krankenhaus? first suggested that they were hitting their stride and now their new album, Valhalla Dancehall, seems like an early contender for album of their year. The Brighton band seems hungry for bigger venues with this bigger sound--though given their history of bad luck with stage diving, hopefully they've learned their lesson about crowd interaction. With A Classic Education.

name: Mike Gordon
description: Anyone's who's ever naively compared Phish's sound to that of the Grateful Dead will find ample evidence in Phish bassist Mike Gordon's solo group. Which isn't to say it's anything less than one of the more deliciously exploratory, viscerally lava lamp-like, and often quite eccentric exemplars of the shrinking jamband subgenre. And if you've ever wondered what Manhattan hippie haven Wetlands sounded (and, perhaps, even smelled) like "back in the day," check out Gordon's two-night stand here and testify, child.

description: There were plenty of exclamation points in the air last year when the sly guitarist figured out how to add horns to her somewhat insular trio. The result was the remarkable Saturn Sings, which found Halvorson's music a bit more appealing without kowtowing to convention. When this group (with Jon Irabagon on sax and Kirk Knuffke on cornet) reaches boiling point, the five-way exchange is a hubbub of cagey design both eccentric and engaging. With Smokey's Roundup.

name: Ladysmith Black Mambazo
description: South Africa's most important vocal ensemble released an album of Zulu children's songs this year, which made sense: they have a broad appeal already, as their lofty lyrical content takes a back seat to their hypnotic harmonizing. Sexagenarian founder Joseph Shabalala is preparing to turn the reins over to his own children, making his project a family affair on both sides. One way or another, this band deserves to last across generations.

name: Totally Enormous Extinct Dinosaurs+Beni+Palms Out Sound DJs
Allman Brothers Band
description: Ah, springtime... Daylight savings happens, trips are planned to SXSW, and the Allmans play about 5,000 shows at their Gotham homebase. They reclaim the Beacon after the venue stupidly gave it to Cirque du Soleil last year, thinking the acrobats would bring more bodies than the jam band crowd. Gregg's in relatively good health again, so let the extended versions of "Whipping Post" unfurl and gawk at the special guests they roll out for each show.
